knowledge.content: Task: Re-implement COBOL program at /app/src/program.cbl in Python at /app/program.py. Must read from /app/src/INPUT.DAT and modify .DAT files in /app/data/ directory (ACCOUNTS.DAT, BOOKS.DAT, TRANSACTIONS.DAT).
Success criteria: Python script output must produce byte-identical .DAT files compared to GnuCOBOL 3 compiled COBOL program, given same inputs and initial file states.
COBOL program designed to run from /app/ directory using GnuCOBOL 3. Three data files in scope: /app/data/ACCOUNTS.DAT, /app/data/BOOKS.DAT, /app/data/TRANSACTIONS.DAT

COBOL program record structures: ACCOUNT-RECORD (ACCOUNT-ID PIC X(4), ACCOUNT-NAME PIC X(20), ACCOUNT-BALANCE PIC 9(10) = 34 bytes total); BOOK-RECORD (BOOK-ID PIC X(4), BOOK-TITLE PIC X(20), BOOK-OWNER PIC X(4) = 28 bytes total); TRANSACTION-RECORD (TRANS-BOOK PIC X(4), TRANS-AMOUNT PIC 9(10), TRANS-SELLER PIC X(4), TRANS-BUYER PIC X(4) = 22 bytes total)

COBOL program logic: 1) Read INPUT.DAT, 2) Validate buyer exists in ACCOUNTS.DAT, 3) Validate seller exists in ACCOUNTS.DAT, 4) Validate book exists in BOOKS.DAT and seller owns it, 5) If all valid: subtract amount from buyer balance, add to seller balance (rewrite ACCOUNTS records), change book owner to buyer (rewrite BOOKS record), append transaction to TRANSACTIONS.DAT. If any validation fails, display error and stop.

COBOL WS-AMOUNT uses PIC 9(10)V99 (decimal with 2 implied decimal places) but INPUT-AMOUNT and TRANS-AMOUNT use PIC 9(10) (integer). COBOL automatically handles conversion. Python must replicate this: input "200" becomes 200 integer, which is stored as-is in transaction file.

COBOL file operations: ACCOUNTS and BOOKS opened with I-O (read-write, updates in-place with REWRITE), TRANSACTIONS opened with EXTEND (append mode), INPUT opened as INPUT (read-only). Files are sequential, processed record-by-record.

INPUT.DAT actual format: File contains only 15 bytes "U001U002B007200" - the amount field "200" is NOT zero-padded to 10 digits in the input file. However, COBOL PIC 9(10) on INPUT-AMOUNT will right-align and zero-pad when reading, so "200" becomes 0000000200.

COBOL DISPLAY statements: Line 119 displays a blank line " " during validation. Line 164 displays "Transaction completed successfully" after successful transaction. Line 80 displays "Transaction failed due to validation errors" if validation fails. Line 64 displays "Error: Input file is empty" if INPUT.DAT is empty. Python must replicate these exact messages.

Python script created at /app/program.py implements: 1) read_input_file() parses 15-byte INPUT.DAT extracting buyer_id (0:4), seller_id (4:8), book_id (8:12), amount (12: as integer), 2) read_accounts_file() and read_books_file() parse fixed-width records, 3) validation checks buyer_found, seller_found, book_found, valid_owner flags, 4) displays blank line before validation result (matching COBOL line 119), 5) if all valid: updates accounts/books in-place, appends to transactions file, displays success; otherwise displays validation error.

procedural.content: Data file byte-level validation complete. Confirmed: INPUT.DAT is 15 bytes (not 22 as record structure would suggest - the 10-digit amount "200" is stored without leading zeros padding, actual content is "U001U002B007200"). ACCOUNTS.DAT records are exactly 34 bytes each (4+20+10), BOOKS.DAT records are 28 bytes each (4+20+4), TRANSACTIONS.DAT records are 22 bytes each (4+10+4+4). All use ASCII encoding with space padding for text fields and zero-padding for numeric fields.

Step 6: COBOL program execution on current INPUT.DAT ("U001U002B007200") resulted in "Transaction failed due to validation errors" message. This indicates at least one validation check failed (buyer not found, seller not found, book not found, or seller doesn't own the book). Need to verify which validation is failing and ensure Python replicates exact same validation logic and display behavior.

Step 7 verification: With INPUT.DAT containing "U001U002B007200", both COBOL and Python programs output " \nTransaction failed due to validation errors" and leave all .DAT files unchanged (verified via MD5 hash comparison). Book B007 does not exist in BOOKS.DAT, causing validation failure. Both implementations correctly handle the validation failure case identically.

Step 8: Created valid test transaction (U001 buys B001 from U002 for amount 150) by writing "U001U002B001150" to INPUT.DAT. COBOL program successfully processes this with output " \nTransaction completed successfully". This confirms: 1) Book B001 exists and is owned by U002, 2) Both U001 and U002 exist in accounts, 3) Transaction processing logic works. Next need to verify Python produces byte-identical results for this valid case.

Step 9: Both COBOL and Python programs successfully process valid test transaction (INPUT.DAT="U001U002B001150"). Both output " \nTransaction completed successfully". COBOL outputs saved to .cobol files for comparison. Need to verify Python-generated data files match COBOL outputs byte-for-byte before testing with original INPUT.DAT.

Step 10: Byte-level comparison reveals differences between COBOL and Python outputs for valid transaction (U001U002B001150). ACCOUNTS.DAT differs in balance values: COBOL shows U001=1499998820 and U002=1500001800, while Python shows U001=0000001030 and U002=0000001950. TRANSACTIONS.DAT also differs in the appended record's amount field. The differences suggest an integer overflow or arithmetic precision issue - COBOL may be treating the amount field differently than Python's straightforward integer arithmetic.

Step 13: COBOL V99 decimal arithmetic test revealed: When SUBTRACT WS-DECIMAL-VAL (PIC 9(10)V99 VALUE 150) FROM WS-INTEGER-VAL (PIC 9(10) VALUE 1180), COBOL correctly produces 1030. When ADD to 1800, produces 1950. This proves COBOL handles V99 to integer conversion correctly in isolation. The actual program bug (producing 1499998820, 1500001800) must stem from something else - likely how WS-AMOUNT gets its value from INPUT-AMOUNT during the MOVE operation at line 73, or file I/O corruption.

Step 16 CRITICAL DISCOVERY: When COBOL reads the 15-byte INPUT.DAT file expecting a 22-byte record with PIC 9(10) amount field, it reads "200" (3 bytes) but the INPUT-AMOUNT field interprets this as 2000000000 (2 billion) instead of 200. The test_read.cbl program shows: INPUT-AMOUNT raw="200" but after MOVE to WS-AMOUNT (PIC 9(10)V99), the value becomes 2000000000.00. This explains the corrupted balance values in ACCOUNTS.DAT (U001=1499998820, U002=1500001800). The 3-byte string "200" left-aligns in the 10-byte numeric field, and the remaining 7 bytes contain uninitialized memory data that COBOL interprets as part of the number.
